708421.t: From Proto-Hellenic *makrós, from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós, from *meh₂ḱ- (“to increase”). By surface analysis, μῆκος (mêkos) + -ρός (-rós).

708491.t: From the root of μαίνομαι (maínomai, “to be mad or raving”), per J.B.

708480.t: From Proto-Hellenic *məntʰánō, *mantʰánō, from Proto-Indo-European *mn̥-n-dʰ-, nasal infix present of *men(s)dʰh₁-, itself possibly a *dʰ-extension of *men- (“to think, mind”), thus "to put one's mind".

708483.t: Formation like μανδάκης (mandákēs) and καυνάκης (kaunákēs). Usually considered to be a Gaulish word, with cognates in Latin monīle (“necklace, collar”) and Proto-Germanic *manją (“collar”).

708497.t: Uncertain. One proposed etymology maintains that the verb derived from Proto-Indo-European *mr̥n̥-ye-ti, a denominative in *-yeti to a nasal-infixed form of the root Proto-Indo-European *mer- (“to die”).

708438.t: Inherited from Proto-Hellenic *məlakos, from Proto-Indo-European *ml̥h₂ekos, from *melh₂- (“soft, weak”), which Beekes separates from the "grind, rub" sense, though this is disputed.

708457.t: Back formed from the onomatopoeic baby-talk μάμμα (mắmmă).

708448.t: From μάλα (mắlă, “very”) + *-ϳον (*-jon, comparative suffix), from Proto-Indo-European *mel- (“strong, big”), with long α (a) perhaps after ἆσσον (âsson). Cognates include Latin melior (“better”).

708433.t: From Proto-Indo-European *mel- (“strong, better”). Cognates include Latin melius, multus and Latvian milns.

708473.t: Some have proposed a Proto-Indo-European *mand- (“enclosure”), cognate with Sanskrit मन्दुरा (mandurā, “stable; bed”) and possibly related to μανδάκης (mandákēs, “band to tie trusses”), μάνδαλος (mándalos, “bolt”), and Proto-West Germanic *mandu…

708411.t: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

708419.t: From μακρόθυμος (măkróthūmos, “long-suffering, patient”) + -ία (-ĭ́ā), from μακρο- (makro-, “long”) + θυμός (thūmós, “soul; temper, passion”).

708474.t: Unexplained. Maybe from Old Persian *merdum gija (“plant of humans”), but it could be a folk-etymological adaptation of a foreign word.
